column4: The section reads “bi-niʿmati rabbik” with the section’s dictionary sense of Rabb as one who brings a favor to completion. This ayah says Allah will complete His favor upon the Prophet and guide him to a straight path, joining completion to the stages of guidance visible in the surah.

The section’s dictionary reading of Rabb completes a favor; here Yaʿqub tells the young Yusuf that Allah will complete His favor upon him and the family of Yaʿqub. The future fulfillment makes the section’s gradual movement from gift to completion concrete.

The section links completion with the endpoint of contentment. This ayah says “I have completed My favor upon you” and joins that completion to Allah’s approval of Islam as religion, giving a direct Quranic instance of favor reaching a settled end.

The section’s central completion claim meets “that He may complete His favor upon you” here: after ablution and purification, Allah gives a manageable practice and names completion of favor as its purpose.

The section treats the final, better outcome as a completed divine favor. In this ayah, the change of prayer direction is followed by “that I may complete My favor upon you,” with guidance as the surrounding purpose; this is another concrete completion of favor through a directed course.

The section’s sense of a favor brought to completion is stated directly in “Thus He completes His favor upon you.” The preceding ayat name shelters, clothing, and protection, so this ayah gathers varied provisions into one completed favor.

The section’s phrase “bi-niʿmati rabbik” recurs exactly in this denial that the Prophet is mad. The same favor formula serves as assurance against slander, clarifying that recounting the gift in 93:11 rests on the Prophet’s divinely given standing.

This ayah repeats the section’s exact phrase “bi-niʿmati rabbik” while denying that the Prophet is a soothsayer or mad. Its own contribution is the paired rejection of accusations, showing the formula’s reassuring use in another passage.

The section’s dictionary entry for root ن ع م gives “anʿama” the sense of increasing. Here Allah promises, “If you are grateful, I will surely increase you,” making gratitude and an increase of favor an explicit relation.

This ayah says “remember Allah’s favor” and then that He “increased you in stature.” The section’s stated dictionary connection between the ن ع م family and increase is made concrete as a granted increase that calls for remembrance.

Sulayman asks to be enabled to thank the favor Allah bestowed on him and his parents, and to do a righteous deed that pleases Him. This directly joins the section’s favor, gratitude, goodness conveyed, and contentment.

The section describes a favor as a good condition and an act of conveying goodness, and 93:11 calls it “your Lord’s favor.” This ayah locates every favor that people have in Allah, grounding the command to recount it in its source.

The section commands recounting the Lord’s favor; this ayah says people recognize Allah’s favor and then deny it. Its exact “niʿmata Allāh” makes denial the direct opposite of the section’s response to favor.

This ayah describes Allah as having “lavished His favors upon you, outward and inward.” The section presents the favor of the Lord as something completed and made known; the visible and hidden scope here shows how much that favor encompasses.

The section’s claim of increasing favor meets this statement that, even if people tried, they could not enumerate Allah’s favor. It supplies the scale of the gift behind the instruction to speak of it.

This repeated Quranic formulation says people cannot count Allah’s favors even if they tried. It makes the section’s image of an increasing, completed favor perceptible as abundance beyond enumeration.

Moses tells his people to remember Allah’s favor upon them, naming prophets, kings, and gifts they had not received from others. This is a communal instance of the section’s command to make the Lord’s favor known.

The section’s root ن ع م is present in “those You have favored,” and the same verse distinguishes their path from the paths of anger and error. That joins favor with guidance, as the surah’s progression from being lost to being guided does.

This ayah uses the section’s root ن ع م in “He made him comfortable,” after expanded provision; the person then concludes “my Lord has honored me.” The next ayat challenge this reading, showing a false equation of comfortable circumstances with honor.

This ayah contributes the opposite misreading: when provision is restricted, the person says his Lord has humiliated him. Its own claim is about constriction; 89:15 supplies the paired claim from plenty, and 89:17 turns from both claims to actual conduct toward the orphan.

After the claims in 89:15–16 that plenty means honor and restriction means humiliation, this ayah answers “No”; it names failure to honor the orphan as the real fault. It connects the section’s definition of inʿām as conveying good to another with the surah’s own care for the vulnerable.

This continuation identifies another failed transfer of goodness: people do not urge one another to feed the poor. The section’s dictionary gloss for inʿām is conveying good to someone else, so the ayah’s concrete provision of food exposes what mere worldly increase fails to accomplish.

The section names the dictionary expression “nuʿmatu al-ʿayn,” the eye’s delight, and points to Moses’s return to his mother. This ayah says he was returned to her “so her eye might be comforted,” making the promised favor a mother’s restored child.

This retelling says Moses was returned to his mother “so her eye might be comforted.” It repeats the section’s specific eye-delight scene and adds that she need not grieve and would know Allah’s promise was true.

Mary is told to eat, drink, and “be comforted in eye” after giving birth. The section’s eye-delight dictionary expression thus appears in another mother-and-child scene, where provision and relief accompany the comfort.

Pharaoh’s wife calls the rescued infant Moses “a comfort of the eye for me and you.” The same child is eye-delight before his return to his mother in 28:13, adding an earlier household’s joy to the section’s return scene.

The section’s dictionary expression for eye delight is echoed by the promised “comforts of eyes” hidden for people as recompense for their deeds. This locates eye-delight in a future gift whose full form remains unseen.

The section glosses “nuʿmatu al-ʿayn” as eye-delight; in this description of Paradise, “eyes delight” alongside whatever souls desire. It connects the section’s idiom to a final provision that meets both sight and desire.

The worshippers pray that their spouses and offspring be “a comfort to our eyes.” This repeats the section’s eye-delight expression in a family setting and makes intimate joy one of the gifts sought from the Lord.

The section says riḍwān is abundant riḍā; this ayah says that if people are grateful, Allah approves their gratitude. Its contrast between human gratitude and ingratitude gives the section’s favor and contentment a reciprocal relation.

The section’s root ر ض و names the Prophet’s contentment after a future gift. Here the one who gives wealth to purify himself and seeks his Lord’s countenance in 92:18–20 “will surely be satisfied”; the same contentment is reached through a distinct act of giving.

The section links divine completion to contentment; this ayah describes the soul returning to its Lord “well-pleased and pleasing.” It gives contentment as the completed end of a life, followed in the next ayat by entry among Allah’s servants and into His garden.

The section explains riḍwān as abundant approval. This ayah names gardens and “approval from Allah” among what is better for the God-conscious, making divine approval part of the better gift beyond worldly desire.

This ayah places “approval from Allah” above the gardens and dwellings promised to believers. It concretely supports the section’s reading of riḍwān as an especially full contentment that crowns other gifts.
The section’s word خَيْر says the Hereafter is better than the first life; this ayah says “the Hereafter is better and more lasting.” It adds endurance to the section’s comparison of the two lives.

This ayah names the contrary preference, that people choose the nearer life; 87:17 supplies the section’s own boundary by saying the Hereafter is better and more lasting. Its contribution is the human preference that the comparison corrects.

The section reads the Hereafter as better than the first life. This ayah says that what people have been given is worldly enjoyment, while what is with Allah is “better and more lasting,” sharpening the contrast between present possession and the better outcome.

This ayah says that what people have been given is worldly enjoyment, while what is with Allah is “better and more lasting” for those who believe and rely on their Lord. It restates the section’s khayr comparison with a specific contrast in what lasts.

The section’s claim that the Hereafter is better than the first life is stated here as the Hereafter’s abode being better for those mindful of God; the worldly life is called play and amusement. It gives the comparison a moral boundary.

This ayah calls the enjoyment of worldly life little and says the Hereafter is better for the God-conscious. It makes the section’s “better for you than the first” comparison concrete through the contrast in lasting reward.

The addressed believers are asked whether they prefer worldly life to the Hereafter, after being called to go forth. It puts the section’s better-after-this-life claim into a direct challenge to the audience’s preference.

This ayah pairs Allah’s expansion and restriction of provision with people rejoicing in worldly life, then calls worldly life only brief enjoyment compared with the Hereafter. It directly links provision’s changing measure to the section’s caution against treating this life as the final good.

The section says khayr is what is desired and the best of things; this ayah contrasts worldly wealth and children with “the enduring good deeds,” which are better with the Lord for reward and hope. It specifies a lasting good rather than a passing possession.

This ayah says that if Allah expanded provision for His servants, they would transgress, so He sends it down in a measure as He wills. It supplies a clear limit to reading abundance as a sign of honor, the mistake named in 89:15.

This ayah says Allah apportions livelihood and raises some people over others for mutual service, then says His mercy is better than what they gather. It makes provision a measured arrangement, not proof that worldly rank is the section’s final good.
This ayah calls worldly life play and amusement and the Hereafter the real life. That is a specific boundary for the section’s claim that the later life is better than the first.

This ayah describes worldly life as play, adornment, boasting, and competition in wealth and children, then contrasts its brief growth and decay with the Hereafter. It illuminates both 93:4’s preference for the later life and 89:15’s mistaken reading of worldly plenty.

The section says the root ر ض و reaches its fullest form in riḍwān and the surah also moves from being lost to guidance. This ayah says the Book guides those who seek Allah’s approval to paths of peace, joining the section’s two details of approval and guidance.

The section’s rida detail has Allah give until the Prophet is content; Moses here says he hurried to his Lord “that You may be pleased.” The direction of seeking approval is reversed, making the mutual relation between gift and contentment visible.

The section describes the sixth-to-eighth ayat as shelter, guidance, and sufficiency, culminating in being enriched. This ayah names Allah as the one who enriches and grants sufficiency, giving a direct parallel for the last step in that progression.

This ayah ends the account of the truthful with gardens and Allah’s approval of them, and their approval of Him. It offers another Quranic form of the section’s contentment as the outcome of divine gift.

The section links riḍwān to full contentment; this ayah joins gardens to Allah’s approval of the believers and theirs of Him. Its own contribution is the reciprocal approval named as the reward of those who fear their Lord.

This ayah says that the people of Paradise will have what they wish from their Lord, as reward for those who do good. It concretizes the section’s description of khayr as what is desired and the future gift that brings contentment.

This ayah says the people of Paradise will have whatever they wish and that Allah has “more.” It provides a specific image of provision exceeding desire, alongside the section’s account of the root ن ع م as increase.
The section’s entry for ن ع م notes a sense of increasing. This ayah says that whoever acquires a good deed will have goodness increased for him, a specific case of good being augmented.

The section’s dictionary account of Rabb includes bringing care to completion. This ayah says Mary’s Lord accepted her well, “grew her with a good growth,” and provided her sustenance; it shows divine care as a developing, sustained provision.

The section explicitly says the root ر ب ب includes raising a child but also completing and improving a favor. This prayer recalls parents who “raised me when small” and asks God for mercy on them, placing the ordinary child-rearing sense beside gratitude for care.

Pharaoh invokes the ordinary child-rearing sense of the section’s root ر ب ب, asking Moses whether “we raised you among us as a child.” His claim is later bounded by Moses’s return to his mother in 20:40, where Allah’s care completes the rescue Pharaoh’s household did not control.

This ayah supplies the fulfillment side of Yusuf’s forecast in 12:6: he recognizes the old dream as made true and names Allah’s kindness in bringing him from prison and his family from the desert. Its own contribution is the realized outcome of the favor promised to the young Yusuf.

The section’s dictionary example for root ر ب ب is tending a plot of land and bringing it to sound completion. This ayah stages a seed growing into many ears and multiplies the return on charitable giving, joining the land image to an increase in good passed onward.

The section’s land-care dictionary sense meets this parable of spending as a garden on high ground, whose yield doubles after rain. It makes a cultivated plot the image of a good act that grows into more provision.

The section’s root entry uses a plot of land as something repaired and brought to completion. This ayah describes rain, grain, palm growth, and gardens emerging from earth, making the land’s productive provision visible.

The section’s land dictionary sense meets this ayah’s gardens, crops, and harvest; it tells people to eat the produce and give its due on harvest day. The field’s completed yield becomes provision passed on to others.

The section describes favors unfolding step by step and cites care of land as a sense of root ر ب ب. This ayah’s seed sends out a shoot, strengthens, thickens, and stands upon its stem, a concrete progression from beginning to mature growth.

The section’s lexicon defines inʿām as conveying goodness to another. This ayah tells Qarun to do good as Allah has done good to him, making receipt of favor explicitly answerable by good directed outward.

The section’s dictionary definition of completing and improving a good deed is made perceptible by this question: “Is the reward of ihsan anything but ihsan?” It joins a well-done good act to its fitting return.

The section defines inʿām as delivering goodness to someone else. This ayah stages that transfer as feeding the needy, orphan, and captive, turning an abstract favor into provision that reaches particular people.

The feeders say that they give only for Allah’s countenance and seek neither repayment nor thanks. That adds a distinct motive to the section’s command to recount Allah’s favor: giving can be directed to God without seeking return from its recipients.
The section says the ن ع م family includes eye-delight and an excellent state. This ayah commands rejoicing in Allah’s bounty and mercy, a specific expression of joy in divine giving.

The section’s dictionary entry for ر ب ب includes bringing land into a sound, productive state. This ayah distinguishes good land whose plants emerge by its Lord’s leave from bad land that yields little, making the land’s response to care a concrete scene.

The section glosses niʿma as a good condition. This ayah promises a “good life” to a believer who does righteous deeds and a reward according to the best of what they did, a specific account of divinely granted well-being.

This parable says a secure town received abundant provision from every place, then became ungrateful for Allah’s favors and tasted hunger and fear. It directly reverses the section’s good state and increasing favor when the gift is denied.

After the account in 16:112–113 of a town that denied Allah’s favor, this ayah commands people to eat good provision and be grateful for Allah’s favor. Its own contribution is the direct pairing of received provision with gratitude.

This ayah states that Allah does not change a favor bestowed on a people until they change what is within themselves. It gives a boundary to the section’s account of a favor completed by its giver: the people’s response matters to what follows.

This ayah says Allah favored the believers by sending them a messenger who recites, purifies, and teaches them, after they had been in clear error. It joins favor to the Prophet’s mission and guidance, matching the section’s connection between divine favor and the stages of being guided.

The ayah calls Abraham grateful for Allah’s favors, says Allah chose him, and says He guided him to a straight path. It repeats the section’s specific meeting of favor, gratitude, and guidance in the account of another prophet.

This ayah says Allah will pay believers’ rewards in full and increase them from His bounty. It brings together the section’s two distinct actions—bringing a good to completion and increasing it—in one promise.

This ayah compares worldly life to rain-grown plants that flourish, then become stubble when Allah’s command arrives, though their owners thought they controlled them. The field scene joins the section’s land dictionary sense to its contrast between passing provision and the better lasting outcome.

The believers are told to remember when they were few, oppressed, and afraid of being seized, then Allah gave them shelter, support, and good provision. This staged movement from vulnerability to safety and provision parallels the section’s shelter, guidance, and sufficiency.

Allah says He intends to favor those oppressed in the land, make them leaders, and make them inheritors. It is a specific staged reversal from low status to an enlarged favor, parallel to the section’s account of provision unfolding through stages.

This ayah explains that the wall concealed treasure for two orphan boys and that their Lord wanted them to reach maturity and recover it, as mercy from Him. It makes divine shelter and provision for vulnerable children concrete, with the benefit kept for a later stage.

Addressing the Prophet, this ayah recalls that he did not know the Book or faith before revelation, then says Allah made the revelation a light by which He guides whom He wills. It is a specific parallel to the section’s movement from an earlier state to divine guidance.

This ayah says people should not grieve over what escapes them or exult over what Allah gives, then warns against boastful pride. It directly limits the false reading in 89:15–16 that worldly increase or restriction by itself signifies honor or humiliation.

The section’s dictionary gloss says khayr is what everyone desires. This ayah supplies a specific boundary: people may dislike what is good for them and love what is bad, so immediate desire does not define the good promised in the section.

This ayah says the bad and the good are not equal, even if the abundance of bad things impresses someone. It sets a concrete boundary on reading worldly quantity as the khayr that the section associates with the better outcome.

The section’s dictionary entry gives tending and improving a plot of land as a sense of root ر ب ب. This ayah describes neighboring plots, gardens, crops, and palms watered by the same water yet producing different fruits, making the land sense concrete.

The section’s lexicon defines inʿām as conveying goodness to another. This ayah makes that transfer specific through commands to do good to parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, neighbors, and travelers.
The section’s entry for ن ع م includes an increase sense. This ayah says a good deed receives ten like it, a specific example of goodness being multiplied rather than merely returned once.

After asking whether a person has whatever he wishes, this ayah says the Hereafter and the first life belong to Allah. It repeats the section’s paired terms and locates the hoped-for good in the giver who owns both lives.

In the surah that later describes a giver who seeks Allah’s face and becomes satisfied, this ayah says the Hereafter and the first life belong to Allah. It repeats the section’s paired terms and frames both outcomes as belonging to the Lord.

Following the promise in 28:5 to favor the oppressed and make them leaders and heirs, this ayah says Allah would establish them in the land and show Pharaoh and Haman what they feared. Its contribution is the promised favor’s concrete realization.

The section describes the Prophet’s life as moving through distinct states before a future gift brings contentment. This ayah gives a specific promise of ease accompanying hardship, which illuminates the transition from need and vulnerability toward sufficiency.

This ayah repeats the preceding promise that ease accompanies hardship. Its contribution is the second assurance in 94:5–6, reinforcing the section’s movement through successive states toward a good outcome.

Moses says he is in need of whatever good his Lord may send down to him. The next ayah brings a man’s invitation and practical help; this one contributes the expressed need that makes the later provision a specific response.

The section’s dictionary definition for root ر ب ب includes making a good deed complete and sound. This ayah says Allah will set people’s deeds right and forgive them, a concrete parallel to soundness and completion of deeds.

This ayah describes one who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient. It reverses the section’s step in which Allah finds the Prophet in need and makes him sufficient: here apparent self-sufficiency accompanies refusal to give.

This ayah describes someone who seeks the immediate life and hurries toward it, receiving only what Allah wills, before facing Hell. It is a specific boundary to the section’s promise that the later life is better than the first.

This ayah contrasts the previous pursuit of immediate life with the person who seeks the Hereafter and strives for it as a believer, whose effort is appreciated. It gives the better outcome a concrete response and reward.

This ayah distinguishes one who seeks the harvest of the Hereafter, whose harvest Allah increases, from one who seeks the harvest of this world and receives only some of it. It joins the section’s increase detail to its comparison of the two lives.

This ayah compares worldly life to rain-grown vegetation that later dries and scatters. The next ayah, 18:46, names worldly wealth and children as adornment and enduring good deeds as better; 18:45 itself contributes the field’s brief flourishing and decay.
